sentence: A Tcl/Tk-based application called GenoMap is described.
GenoMap is a viewer for genome-wide map of microarray expression data within a circular bacterial genome.
An interactive interface facilitates easy identification of the expressed region.
This software is used for drawing genome-wide quantitative data.
Genome2D is a Windows-based software tool for visualization of bacterial transcriptome and customized datasets on linear chromosome maps constructed from annotated genome sequences.
Genome2D facilitates the analysis of transcriptome data by using different color ranges to depict differences in gene-expression levels on a genome map.
The output format of Genome2D enables visual inspection of the transcriptome data.
Genome2D quickly reveals transcriptional units without prior knowledge of expression level cutoff values.
The compiled version of Genome2D is freely available for academic or non-profit use from http://molgen.biol.rug.nl/molgen/research/molgensoftware.php.
CGView (Circular Genome Viewer) is a Java application and library for generating high-quality, zoomable maps of circular genomes.
CGView converts XML or tab-delimited input into a graphical map in PNG, JPG, or Scalable Vector Graphics format.
The graphical map includes sequence features, labels, legends, and footnotes.
In addition to the default full view map, the program can generate a series of hyperlinked maps showing expanded views.
The linked maps can be explored using any Web browser.
The linked maps allow rapid genome browsing and facilitate data sharing.
CGView is available as a standalone application, library, or applet.
Sample input, sample maps, and documentation for CGView can be obtained from http://wishart.biology.ualberta.ca/cgview/.
BacMap is an interactive visual database containing fully labeled, zoomable, and searchable chromosome maps from more than 170 bacterial species.
BacMap includes chromosome maps from both archaebacterial and eubacterial species.
BacMap uses a recently developed visualization tool (CGView) to generate high-resolution circular genome maps from sequence feature information.
Each map includes an interface that allows the image to be expanded and rotated.
In the default view, identified genes are drawn to scale and colored according to coding directions.
When a region of interest is expanded, gene labels are displayed.
Each gene label is hyperlinked to a custom 'gene card' which provides several fields of information concerning the corresponding DNA and protein sequences.
Each genome map is searchable via a local BLAST search and a gene name/synonym search.
BacMap is freely available at http://wishart.biology.ualberta.ca/BacMap/.
DNAPlotter is an interactive Java application for generating circular and linear representations of genomes.
DNAPlotter makes use of the Artemis libraries to provide a user-friendly method of loading in sequence files (EMBL, GenBank, GFF) as well as data from relational databases.
DNAPlotter filters features of interest to display on separate user-definable tracks.
DNAPlotter can be used to produce publication quality images for papers or web pages.
DNAPlotter is freely available under a GPL licence.
DNAPlotter can be downloaded for MacOSX, UNIX, and Windows.
DNAPlotter is available at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute websites.
The download link for DNAPlotter is http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Software/Artemis/circular/.
Circoletto is an online visualization tool.
Circoletto is based on Circos.
Circoletto provides a fast, aesthetically pleasing, and informative overview of sequence similarity search results.
An online version and downloadable software package for offline use are available.
The source code is written in PERL.
The software is freely available at http://bat.ina.certh.gr/tools/circoletto/.
A novel, interactive visualization model for comparative analysis of structural variants and rearrangements in human and cancer genomes is presented, applied, and evaluated.
The model emphasizes data integration and uncertainty visualization.
The model supports both global trend analysis and local feature detection.
The model enables explorations continuously scaled from the high-level, complete genome perspective to the low-level, structural rearrangement view, while preserving global context.
These techniques have been implemented in Gremlin, a genomic rearrangement explorer with multi-scale, linked interactions.
Gremlin is applied to four human cancer genome datasets for evaluation.
An insight-based evaluation methodology is used to compare Gremlin to Circos, the state-of-the-art in genomic rearrangement visualization.
A small user study with computational biologists working in rearrangement analysis is conducted.

Results from user study evaluations demonstrate that this visualization model enables more total insights than the current state-of-the-art for visual analysis and exploration of genome rearrangements.
The visualization model enables more insights per minute than the current state-of-the-art for visual analysis and exploration of genome rearrangements.
The visualization model enables more complex insights than the current state-of-the-art for visual analysis and exploration of genome rearrangements.
phiGENOME is a web-based genome browser generating dynamic and interactive graphical representation of phage genomes stored in the phiSITE database.
phiSITE is a database of gene regulation in bacteriophages.
phiGENOME is an integral part of the phiSITE web portal (http://www.phisite.org/phigenome).
phiGENOME was optimised for visualisation of phage genomes with an emphasis on gene regulatory elements.
phiGENOME consists of three components: genome map viewer, sequence browser, and regulation illustrator.
The genome map viewer is built using Adobe Flash technology and provides dynamic and interactive graphical display of phage genomes.
The sequence browser is based on precisely formatted HTML tags and provides detailed exploration of genome features on the sequence level.
The regulation illustrator is based on Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) and is designed for graphical representation of gene regulations.
phiGENOME brings 542 complete genome sequences accompanied with their rich annotations and references.
phiGENOME is a unique information resource in the field of phage genomics.
Several studies have shown how sets of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) can help to classify subjects on the basis of their continental origins.
This classification has applications to case-control studies and population genetics.
Most of these studies use dimensionality-reduction methods, such as principal component analysis, or clustering methods.
These methods result in unipartite (either subjects or SNPs) representations of the data.
Unipartite analyses conceal important bipartite relationships, such as how subject and SNP clusters relate to each other.
Unipartite analyses also conceal the genotypes that determine their cluster memberships.
Current methods of analyzing SNP data have limitations.
The authors used three bipartite analytical representations: bipartite network, heat map with dendrograms, and Circos ideogram.
These representations enable the simultaneous visualization and analysis of subjects, SNPs, and subject attributes.
The results demonstrate novel insights into SNP data that are difficult to derive from purely unipartite views of the data.
The results reveal the strengths and limitations of each method.
The results reveal the role that each method plays in revealing novel insights.
The results have implications for how the methods can be used for the analysis of SNPs in genomic studies associated with disease.
Bipartite representations can reveal new patterns in SNP data compared with existing unipartite representations.
Novel insights require multiple representations to discover, verify, and comprehend complex relationships.
The results motivate the need for a complementary visual analytical framework.
The framework guides the use of multiple bipartite representations to analyze complex relationships in SNP data.
The evolutionary pressures that underlie the large-scale functional organization of the genome are not well understood in eukaryotes.
Recent evidence suggests that functionally similar genes may colocalize (cluster) in the eukaryotic genome.
Gene colocalization suggests the role of chromatin-level gene regulation in shaping the physical distribution of coordinated genes.
Few of the bioinformatic tools currently available allow for a systematic study of gene colocalization across several, evolutionarily distant species.
Most bioinformatic tools require the user to input manually curated lists of gene position information, DNA sequence, or gene homology relations between species.
With the growing number of sequenced genomes, there is a need to provide new comparative genomics tools that can address the analysis of multi-species gene colocalization.
Kerfuffle is a web tool designed to help discover, visualize, and quantify the physical organization of genomes.
Kerfuffle identifies significant gene colocalization and conservation across the assembled genomes of available species.
Kerfuffle currently supports up to 47 species, ranging from humans to worms.
Kerfuffle only requires the user to specify a list of human genes and the names of other species of interest.
The software queries the e!Ensembl BioMart server to obtain positional information and discovers homology relations in all genes and species specified.
Kerfuffle performs a multi-species clustering analysis using the obtained information.
Kerfuffle presents downloadable lists of clustered genes.
Kerfuffle performs Monte Carlo statistical significance calculations.
Kerfuffle estimates how conserved gene clusters are across species.
Kerfuffle plots histograms and interactive graphs.
Kerfuffle allows users to save their queries.
Kerfuffle generates a downloadable visualization of the clusters using the Circos software.
These analyses may be used to further explore the functional roles of gene clusters.
The functional roles of gene clusters can be interrogated by exploring the enriched molecular pathways associated with each cluster.
Kerfuffle is a new, easy-to-use and publicly available tool to aid understanding of functional genomics and comparative genomics.
Kerfuffle allows for flexibility and quick investigations of a user-defined set of genes.
The results from Kerfuffle may be saved online for further analysis.
Kerfuffle is freely available at http://atwallab.org/kerfuffle.
Kerfuffle is implemented in JavaScript using jQuery and jsCharts libraries.
Kerfuffle is implemented in PHP 5.2.
Kerfuffle runs on an Apache server.
Kerfuffle stores data in flat files and an SQLite database.

Cancer genomics projects employ high-throughput technologies to identify the complete catalog of somatic alterations that characterize the genome, transcriptome, and epigenome of cohorts of tumor samples.
Examples of cancer genomics projects include those carried out by the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
A crucial step in the extraction of knowledge from cancer genomics data is the exploration by experts of the different alterations and the multiple relationships between them.
The use of intuitive visualization tools that can integrate different types of alterations with clinical data is essential to the field of cancer genomics.
This review discusses effective and common visualization techniques for exploring oncogenomics data.
The review highlights tools that allow researchers to effectively visualize multidimensional oncogenomics datasets.
Visualization methods employed by tools such as Circos, Gitools, the Integrative Genomics Viewer, Cytoscape, Savant Genome Browser, and StratomeX are covered.
Platforms such as cBio Cancer Genomics Portal, IntOGen, the UCSC Cancer Genomics Browser, the Regulome Explorer, and the Cancer Genome Workbench are also discussed.
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have enabled high-throughput and low-cost generation of sequence data.
De novo genome assembly remains a great challenge, particularly for large genomes.
NGS short reads are often insufficient to create large contigs that span repeat sequences and to facilitate unambiguous assembly.

Plant genomes are notorious for containing high quantities of repetitive elements, which combined with huge genome sizes, makes accurate assembly of these large and complex genomes intractable thus far.

Using two-color genome mapping of tiling bacterial artificial chromosomes (BAC) clones on nanochannel arrays, we completed high-confidence assembly of a 2.1-Mb, highly repetitive region in the large and complex genome of Aegilops tauschii, the D-genome donor of hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum).
Genome mapping is based on direct visualization of sequence motifs on single DNA molecules hundreds of kilobases in length.
With the genome map as a scaffold, we anchored unplaced sequence contigs, validated the initial draft assembly, and resolved instances of misassembly, some involving contigs <2 kb long.
We dramatically improved the assembly from 75% to 95% complete.
Homozygosity mapping has been widely applied to identify disease variants and investigate the effects of genome-wide homozygosity regions on traits of biomedical importance.
Existing methods and algorithms to identify long tracts of homozygosity (TOH) are not able to provide efficient and rigorous regions for downstream association investigation.
We expanded current methods to identify TOHs by defining 'surrogate-TOH', a region covering a cluster of TOHs with specific characteristics.
Surrogate-TOH includes cTOH, a common TOH region where at least ten TOHs are present.
Surrogate-TOH includes gTOH, a group of highly overlapping TOHs that share proximal boundaries.
Surrogate-TOH includes aTOH, which are allelically-matched TOHs.
Searching for gTOH and aTOH was based on a repeated binary spectral clustering algorithm.
A hierarchy of clusters is created and represented by a TOH cluster tree.
Based on the proposed method of identifying different species of surrogate-TOH, our cgaTOH software was developed.
The cgaTOH software provides an intuitive and interactive visualization tool for better investigation of high-throughput output with special interactive navigation rings.
The cgaTOH software will find its applicability in both conventional association studies and more sophisticated downstream analyses.
NCBI genome map viewer is incorporated into the cgaTOH system.
We discuss the choice of implementing appropriate empirical ranges of critical parameters by applying the method to disease models.
This method identifies various patterned clusters of SNPs demonstrating extended homozygosity.
The method allows observation of different aspects of the multi-faceted characteristics of TOHs.

MISTIC is a web server for graphical representation of the information contained within a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and a complete analysis tool for Mutual Information networks in protein families.
The server outputs a graphical visualization of several information-related quantities using a circos representation.
The graphical visualization provides an integrated view of the MSA in terms of mutual information (MI) between residue pairs, sequence conservation, and residue cumulative and proximity MI scores.
An interactive interface to explore and characterize the MI network is provided.
Several tools are offered for selecting subsets of nodes from the network for visualization.
Node coloring can be set to match different attributes, such as conservation, cumulative MI, proximity MI, and secondary structure.
A zip file containing all results can be downloaded.
The server is available at http://mistic.leloir.org.ar.
MISTIC allows for a comprehensive, compact, visually rich view of the information contained within an MSA in a manner unique to any other publicly available web server.
The use of circos representation of MI networks and the visualization of the cumulative MI and proximity MI concepts is novel.
Visualization plays an essential role in genomics research by making it possible to observe correlations and trends in large datasets.
Visualization helps communicate findings to others.
Visual analysis combines visualization with analysis tools to enable seamless use of both approaches for scientific investigation.
Visual analysis offers a powerful method for performing complex genomic analyses.
Creating rich, interactive Web-based visualizations/visual analysis applications for high-throughput genomics presents numerous challenges.
Challenges include managing data flow from Web server to Web browser.
Challenges include integrating analysis tools and visualizations.
Challenges include sharing visualizations with colleagues.
A platform was created to simplify the creation of Web-based visualization and visual analysis applications for high-throughput genomics.
The platform provides components to efficiently query very large datasets.
The platform provides components to draw common representations of genomic data.
The platform provides components to integrate with analysis tools.
The platform provides components to share or publish fully interactive visualizations.
Using the platform, a Circos-style genome-wide viewer was created.
Using the platform, a generic scatter plot for correlation analysis was created.
Using the platform, an interactive phylogenetic tree was created.
Using the platform, a scalable genome browser for next-generation sequencing data was created.
Using the platform, an application for systematically exploring tool parameter spaces to find good parameter values was created.
All visualizations created using the platform are interactive and fully customizable.
The platform is integrated with the Galaxy genomics workbench.
The integration with Galaxy makes it easy to integrate new visual applications into Galaxy.
Visualization and visual analysis play an important role in high-throughput genomics experiments.
Approaches are needed to make it easier to create applications for visualization and visual analysis in high-throughput genomics experiments.
Our framework provides a foundation for creating Web-based visualizations.
Our framework integrates Web-based visualizations into Galaxy.
The visualizations created using the framework are useful tools for high-throughput genomics experiments.
Targeted sequencing using next-generation sequencing technologies is being rapidly adopted for clinical sequencing and cancer marker tests.
No existing bioinformatics tool is available for the analysis and visualization of multiple targeted sequencing datasets.
The study uses cancer panel targeted sequencing datasets generated by the Life Technologies Ion Personal Genome Machine Sequencer as an example.
The study illustrates how to develop an automated pipeline for the comparative analyses of multiple datasets.
Cancer Panel Analysis Pipeline (CPAP) uses standard output files from variant calling software to generate a distribution map of SNPs among all samples in a circular diagram generated by Circos.
The circular diagram is hyperlinked to a dynamic HTML table that allows users to identify target SNPs using different filters.
CPAP integrates additional information about identified SNPs by linking to an integrated SQL database compiled from SNP-related databases, including dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, COSMIC, and dbNSFP.
CPAP completes a comparative analysis of 500 datasets in only 17 minutes.
CPAP provides an automated platform for the analysis of multiple cancer panel datasets.
CPAP can serve as a model for any customized targeted sequencing project.
Circos is a Perl language-based software package for visualizing similarities and differences of genome structure and positional relationships between genomic intervals.
Running Circos requires extra data processing procedures to prepare plot data files and configure files from datasets.
This requirement limits Circos' capability of integrating directly with other software tools such as R.
The recently published R Bioconductor package ggbio provides a function to display genomic data in circular layout based on multiple other packages.
The use of multiple packages in ggbio increases its complexity of usage.
The complexity of ggbio decreases its flexibility in integrating with other R pipelines.
We implemented an R package, RCircos.
RCircos uses only R packages that come with the R base installation.
The package supports Circos 2D data track plots such as scatter, line, histogram, heatmap, tile, connectors, links, and text labels.
Each plot is implemented with a specific function.
Input data for all functions are data frames.
Data frames can be objects read from text files or generated with other R pipelines.
The RCircos package provides a simple and flexible way to make Circos 2D track plots with R.
The RCircos package can be easily integrated into other R data processing and graphic manipulation pipelines for presenting large-scale multi-sample genomic research data.
The RCircos package can serve as a base tool to generate complex Circos images.
Many tools are available to study variation and its impact in single genomes.
There is a lack of algorithms for finding variation in metagenomes.
This lack hampers the interpretation of metagenomics sequencing datasets.
Metagenomics sequencing datasets are increasingly acquired in research on the human microbiome, in environmental studies, and in the study of processes in the production of foods and beverages.
Existing algorithms often depend on the use of reference genomes.
The use of reference genomes poses a problem when a metagenome of a priori unknown strain composition is studied.
We develop a method to perform reference-free detection and visual exploration of genomic variation.
The method can detect genomic variation both within a single metagenome and between metagenomes.
The MaryGold algorithm efficiently detects bubble structures in contig graphs using graph decomposition.
Bubble structures represent variable genomic regions in closely related strains in metagenomic samples.
The variation found is presented in a condensed Circos-based visualization.
The Circos-based visualization allows for easy exploration and interpretation of the found variation.
The algorithm was validated on two simulated datasets containing three and seven Escherichia coli genomes, respectively.
Finding allelic variation in these genomes improves assemblies.
MaryGold was applied to publicly available real metagenomic datasets.

MaryGold enabled the detection of within-sample genomic variation in the metagenomes of a kimchi fermentation process, the microbiome of a premature infant, and microbial communities living on acid mine drainage.
MaryGold was used for between-sample variation detection and exploration by comparing sequencing data sampled at different time points for both datasets.
MaryGold has been written in C++ and Python.
MaryGold can be downloaded from http://bioinformatics.tudelft.nl/software.
Detection of large genomic rearrangements, such as large indels, duplications, or translocations, is now commonly achieved by next generation sequencing (NGS) approaches.
Several tools have been developed recently to analyze NGS data.
The resulting files from NGS data analysis are difficult to interpret without an additional visualization step.
Circos is a powerful visualization software that requires setting up numerous configuration files with a large number of parameters to handle.
Circos is a Perl script for visualizing genomic data.
R packages like RCircos or ggbio provide functions to display genomic data as circular Circos-like plots.
RCircos and ggbio are very general tools and lack the functions needed to filter, format, and adjust specific input genomic data.
An R package called CIRCUS was implemented to analyze genomic structural variations.
CIRCUS generates both data and configuration files necessary for Circos to produce graphs.
Only a few R pre-requisites are necessary to use CIRCUS.
CIRCUS provides options to handle heterogeneous data.
CIRCUS supports various chromosome numbers and multi-scale analysis.
CIRCUS allows fast analysis of genomic structural variants.
CIRCUS provides versatile analysis of genomic structural variants.
CIRCUS uses Circos plots for visualization.
CIRCUS is designed for users with limited coding skills.
Circleator is a Perl application that generates circular figures of genome-associated data.
Circleator leverages BioPerl to support standard annotation and sequence file formats.
Circleator produces publication-quality SVG output.
Circleator is designed to be both flexible and easy to use.
Circleator includes a library of circular track types and predefined configuration files for common use-cases.
Circleator can visualize gene annotation and DNA sequence data from a GenBank flat file.
Circleator can display patterns of gene conservation in related microbial strains.
Circleator can show Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) and indels relative to a reference genome and gene set.
Circleator can view RNA-Seq plots.
Circleator is freely available under the Artistic License 2.0.
Circleator is available from http://jonathancrabtree.github.io/Circleator/.
Circleator is integrated with the CloVR cloud-based sequence analysis Virtual Machine (VM).
The CloVR Virtual Machine (VM) can be downloaded from http://clovr.org.
The CloVR Virtual Machine (VM) can be run on Amazon EC2.
Circos plots are graphical outputs that display three-dimensional chromosomal interactions and fusion transcripts.
The Circos plot tool is not an interactive visualization tool, but rather a figure generator.
The Circos plot tool does not enable data to be added dynamically.
The Circos plot tool does not provide information for specific data points interactively.
An R-based Circos tool (RCircos) has been developed to integrate Circos to R.
RCircos can only be used to generate plots.
We have developed a Circos plot tool (J-Circos) that is an interactive visualization tool.
J-Circos can plot Circos figures, dynamically add data to the figure, and provide information for specific data points using mouse hover display and zoom in/out functions.
J-Circos uses the Java computer language to enable it to be used on most operating systems (Windows, MacOS, Linux).
Users can input data into J-Circos using flat data formats.
Users can input data into J-Circos from the Graphical User Interface (GUI).
J-Circos will enable biologists to better study more complex chromosomal interactions and fusion transcripts.
These chromosomal interactions and fusion transcripts are otherwise difficult to visualize from next-generation sequencing data.
J-circos and its manual are freely available at http://www.australianprostatecentre.org/research/software/jcircos.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
CiVi is a user-friendly web-based tool to create custom circular maps for analyzing microbial genomes and sequence elements.
Sequence-related data such as gene-name, COG class, PFAM domain, GC%, and subcellular location can be comprehensively viewed using CiVi.
Quantitative gene-related data, such as expression ratios or read counts, can be uploaded and visualized in CiVi.
Predicted sequence elements, such as regulatory sequences, can also be uploaded and visualized in CiVi.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of their genome-wide distribution.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of provided experimental data.
CiVi allows visual interpretation of genomic elements in the context of their local orientation and location with respect to neighboring genes.
CiVi enables both experts and non-experts to integrate public genome data with the results of genome analyses in circular genome maps suitable for publication.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
CiVi is freely available at http://civi.cmbi.ru.nl.
Interprotein contact prediction using multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) is a useful approach to help detect protein-protein interfaces.
Different computational methods have been developed in recent years as an approximation to solve the problem of interprotein contact prediction.
There are discrepancies in the results provided by different computational methods for interprotein contact prediction.
There is still no consensus on which is the best performing methodology for interprotein contact prediction.
I-COMS (interprotein COrrelated Mutations Server) is presented to address the problem of interprotein contact prediction.
I-COMS allows estimation of covariation between residues of different proteins using four different covariation methods.
I-COMS provides a graphical and interactive output to compare results obtained using different covariation methods.
I-COMS automatically builds the required MSA for the calculation.
I-COMS produces a rich visualization of intraprotein and/or interprotein covariating positions in a circos representation.
I-COMS allows comparison between any two covariation methods and the overlap between any or all four methodologies.
I-COMS provides a matrix visualization of the corresponding scores as a complementary source of information.
I-COMS calculates the density plot distribution of inter, intra, and inter+intra scores.
All results from I-COMS, including MSAs, scores, and graphics, can be downloaded for comparison, visualization, and further analysis.
Genome browsers supply vast amounts of information about proteins.
Protein databanks supply vast amounts of information about proteins.
The challenge is to concisely bring together protein information in an interactive format.
The challenge is to concisely bring together protein information in an easy to generate format.
An interactive CIRCOS module called i-PV has been developed.
I-PV visualizes user-supplied protein sequence, conservation, and SNV data in a live presentable format.
I-PV can be downloaded from http://www.i-pv.org.
Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
MicroRNAs are a newly discovered class of non-protein small RNAs with 22-24 nucleotides.
MicroRNAs play multiple roles in biological processes including development, cell proliferation, apoptosis, stress responses, and many other cell functions.
Several approaches were combined to make a computational prediction of potential miRNAs and their targets in Helianthus annuus (H. annuus).
The already available information of the plant miRNAs present in miRBase v21 was used against expressed sequence tags (ESTs).
A total of three miRNAs were detected.
One potential novel miRNA was identified following a range of strict filtering criteria.
The target prediction was carried out for these three miRNAs having various targets.
These targets were functionally annotated and GO terms were assigned.
Predicted phylogenetic analysis was carried out to study the conserved nature of the miRNAs.
These findings will significantly provide the broader picture for understanding the functions in H. annuus.
Glioma is often diagnosed at a later stage, and the high risk of recurrence remains a major challenge.
The microRNA expression profile may serve as a biomarker for the prognosis and prediction of glioblastoma recurrence.
MicroRNAs associated with good and poor prognosis were defined in 300 specimens of glioblastoma from the Cancer Genome Atlas.
Microarray gene expression data and clinical information from three random groups were analyzed.
Seven microRNAs with prognostic and prognostic accuracy were identified: microRNA-124a, microRNA-129, microRNA-139, microRNA-15b, microRNA-21, microRNA-218, and microRNA-7.
The differential expression of these miRNAs was verified using an independent set of glioma samples from the Affiliated People's Hospital of Jiangsu University.
The log-rank test and the Kaplan-Meier method were used to estimate correlations between the miRNA signature and disease-free survival/overall survival.
Using the LASSO model, a uniform significant difference in disease-free survival and overall survival was observed between patients with high-risk and low-risk miRNA signature scores.
The prognostic capability of the seven-miRNA signature was demonstrated by receiver operator characteristic curve analysis.
A Circos plot was generated to examine the network of genes and pathways predicted to be targeted by the seven-miRNA signature.
The seven-miRNA-based classifier should be useful in the stratification and individualized management of patients with glioma.
Quality control and normalization is considered the most important step in the analysis of microarray data.
Various methods are available for quality assessments of microarray datasets.
There is no standard visualization routine that depicts individual microarray quality.
A convenient method for visualizing the results of standard quality control tests using Circos plots is presented.
In Circos plots, various quality measurements are drawn in a circular fashion, allowing for visualization of the quality and all outliers of each distinct array within a microarray dataset.
The proposed method is intended for use with the Affymetrix Human Genome platform (i.e., GPL96, GPL570, and GPL571).
Circos quality measurement plots are a convenient way for the initial quality estimate of Affymetrix datasets stored in publicly available databases.
The global shift toward non-communicable diseases overlaps with the unfinished agenda of confronting infectious diseases in low- and middle-income countries.
Epidemiological links across non-communicable and infectious disease burdens must be recognized.
This study examined the non-communicable disease-infectious disease overlap in specific comorbidity rates.
The study focused on key diseases in an occupational cohort in Papua, Indonesia.

Diagnosed cases of ischaemic heart disease, stroke, hypertension, diabetes (types 1 and 2), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, cancer, HIV and AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria were extracted from 22,550 patient records.
The patient records included 21,513 men and 1,037 women.
The records were stored in identical electronic health information systems from two clinic sites in Papua, Indonesia.
Data were collected as International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, entries from records spanning January-December 2013.
A novel application of Circos software was used to visualize the interconnectedness between the disease burdens.
The visualization represented overlapping prevalence estimates as comorbidities.
Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) represented 38% of all disease cases.
Type 2 diabetes accounted for 1440 cases of NCDs.
Hypertension accounted for 1398 cases of NCDs.
Malaria cases represented the largest single portion of the disease burden with 5310 recorded cases.
Type 2 diabetes was the second largest contributor to the disease burden with 1400 cases.
Tuberculosis occurred most frequently alongside malaria, accounting for 29% of cases.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease occurred alongside tuberculosis in 19% of cases.
Asthma occurred alongside tuberculosis in 17% of cases.
Stroke occurred alongside tuberculosis in 12% of cases.
Hypertension-tuberculosis comorbidities accounted for 4% of cases.
Tuberculosis-cancer comorbidities accounted for 4% of cases.
Asthma-tuberculosis comorbidities accounted for 2% of cases.
The high prevalence of multimorbidity is highlighted in this cohort of mining workers in Papua, Indonesia.
There is a preponderance of non-communicable diseases in this cohort of mining workers in Papua, Indonesia.
Extensive interweaving of non-communicable and infectious disease comorbidities is observed in this cohort of mining workers in Papua, Indonesia.
This reflects the markedly double disease burden increasingly plaguing Indonesia and other similar low- and middle-income countries.
Over-stretched, under-resourced health systems in these countries are ill-equipped to cope with this challenge.
Integrated, person-centered treatment and control strategies rooted in the primary healthcare sector will be critical to reverse this trend.

The objective of this study was to identify genomic regions and metabolic pathways associated with dry matter intake, average daily gain, feed efficiency, and residual feed intake in an experimental Nellore cattle population.
The high-density SNP chip (Illumina High-Density Bovine BeadChip, 777k) was used to genotype the animals.
The SNP markers effects and their variances were estimated using the single-step genome-wide association method.
The (co)variance components were estimated by Bayesian inference.
Chromosome segments responsible for more than 1.0% of additive genetic variance were selected to explore and determine possible quantitative trait loci.
The bovine genome Map Viewer was used to identify genes.
In total, 51 genomic regions were identified for all analyzed traits.
The heritability estimated for feed efficiency was of low magnitude (0.13±0.06).
The heritability estimated for average daily gain was moderate to high (0.43±0.05).
The heritability estimated for dry matter intake was moderate to high (0.47±0.05).
The heritability estimated for residual feed intake was moderate to high (0.18±0.05).
A total of 8 windows responsible for more than 1% of the additive genetic variance for dry matter intake were identified.
A total of 17 windows responsible for more than 1% of the additive genetic variance for average daily gain were identified.
A total of 14 windows responsible for more than 1% of the additive genetic variance for feed efficiency were identified.
A total of 12 windows responsible for more than 1% of the additive genetic variance for residual feed intake were identified.
Candidate genes GOLIM4, RFX6, CACNG7, CACNG6, CAPN8, CAPN2, AKT2, GPRC6A, and GPR45 were associated with feed efficiency traits.
It was expected that the response to selection would be higher for residual feed intake than for feed efficiency.
Genomic regions harboring possible QTL for feed efficiency indicator traits were identified.
Candidate genes identified are involved in energy use, metabolism protein, ion transport, transmembrane transport, the olfactory system, the immune system, secretion, and cellular activity.
The identification of these regions and their respective candidate genes should contribute to the formation of a genetic basis in Nellore cattle for feed efficiency indicator traits.
These results would support the selection for these traits.
This chapter describes methods currently available for visualizing results from systems genetics experiments.
The statistical methods used for genetic mapping depend on the specific resource being used, such as F2, RILs, or outbred populations.
A public dataset with results from a mouse eQTL experiment is used for three examples of visualization.

RISE is a database of RNA Interactome from Sequencing Experiments.
RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are essential for RNA regulation and function.
RISE provides a comprehensive collection of RRIs from transcriptome-wide sequencing-based experiments like PARIS, SPLASH, LIGR-seq, and MARIO.
RISE also includes RRIs from targeted studies like RIA-seq, RAP-RNA, and CLASH.
RISE aggregates interactions from other primary databases and publications.
The RISE database currently contains 328,811 RNA-RNA interactions mainly in human, mouse, and yeast.
More than half of the RRIs in RISE are among mRNA and long non-coding RNAs, unlike most existing RNA databases that mainly contain interactions of miRNA targeting.
We compared different RRI datasets in RISE and found limited overlaps in interactions resolved by different techniques and in different cell lines.
The limited overlaps in RRI datasets may suggest technology preference and dynamic natures of RRIs.
The basic features of human and mouse RRI networks were analyzed and found to be scale-free, small-world, hierarchical, and modular.
The analysis of RRI networks may nominate important RNAs or RRIs for further investigation.

RISE includes extensive molecular and functional annotations to facilitate exploration of biological functions for any RRI of interest.

Biofilms play an important role in antibiotic drug resistance, which is threatening public health globally.
Almost all microbes mimic a multicellular lifestyle to form biofilm by undergoing phenotypic changes to adapt to adverse environmental conditions.
Many anti-biofilm agents have been experimentally validated to disrupt biofilms during the last three decades.
We developed the 'aBiofilm' resource (http://bioinfo.imtech.res.in/manojk/abiofilm/) to organize this data.

The database contains biological, chemical, and structural details of 5027 anti-biofilm agents (1720 unique) reported from 1988-2017.

The agents are mainly chemicals, peptides, phages, secondary metabolites, antibodies, nanoparticles, and extracts.

Hi-C is a proximity-based ligation reaction used to detect regions of the genome that are close in 3D space.
Hi-C results, known as contact maps, are typically visualized as heatmaps or Circos plots.
These visualizations do not directly represent genomic structure and folding.
The interpretation of the underlying 3D genomic organization is obscured by these visualizations.
Our objective was to generate a graph-based contact map representation.
The graph-based contact map representation leads to a more intuitive structural visualization.

Normalized contact maps were converted into undirected graphs where each vertex represented a genomic region and each edge represented a detected (intra- and inter-chromosomal) or known (linear) interaction between two regions.
Each edge was weighted by the inverse of the linear distance (Hi-C experimental resolution) or the interaction frequency from the contact map.
Graphs were generated based on this representation scheme for contact maps from existing fission yeast datasets.
The existing fission yeast datasets were originally used to identify specific principles influencing fission yeast genome organization.
The existing fission yeast datasets were originally used to uncover changes in fission yeast genome organization during the cell cycle.
When compared to the equivalent heatmaps and/or Circos plots, the graph-based visualizations more intuitively depicted the changes in genome organization described in the original studies.

Incidence and mortality of lung cancer have dramatically decreased during the last decades.
Approximately 160,000 deaths per year occurred in the United States due to lung cancer.
Smoking intensity, duration, starting age, as well as environmental cofactors including air pollution, showed strong association with major types of lung cancer.
Lung squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, which represents 25% of the cases.
Exploring the molecular pathogenic mechanisms of lung squamous cell carcinoma plays crucial roles in lung cancer clinical diagnosis and therapy.
Integrative analyses were performed on 299 comparative datasets of RNA-seq and methylation data.
The datasets were collected from 513 lung squamous cell carcinoma cases in The Cancer Genome Atlas.
The data were divided into high and low smoking groups based on smoking intensity (numbers of packs per year).
1002 significantly up-regulated genes and 534 significantly down-regulated genes were identified.
The cellular functions and signaling pathways of these genes were explored using bioconductor packages GOseq and KEGG.
Global methylation status was analyzed and visualized in a circular plot using CIRCOS.
RNA and methylation data were correlatively analyzed, identifying 24 unique genes.
Regional CpG sites' interactive patterns were further investigated using the bioconductor package coMET.
AIRE, PENK, and SLC6A3 were the top 3 genes with significant differences between the high and low smoking groups.
Gene functions of these 24 genes are important in disclosing differences in gene expression caused by different smoking levels.
DNA methylation patterns of these 24 genes are useful in disclosing differences in methylation profiling caused by different smoking levels.
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common disease of the digestive system with no curative treatments.
Long noncoding RNA tyrosine protein kinase transmembrane receptor 1 antisense RNA 1 (lncRNA ROR1‑AS1) is an lncRNA whose functions have been predicted in human diseases.
The role of lncRNA ROR1‑AS1 in cancer has been probed only in mantle cell lymphoma, not in HCC.
The present study aimed to elucidate the prognostic significance of lncRNA ROR1‑AS1 in HCC.
The Cancer Genome Atlas Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma was used to analyze the expression of ROR1‑AS1 in liver cancer.
χ2 tests were performed to evaluate associations between clinical characteristics and ROR1‑AS1 expression.
The role of ROR1‑AS1 in HCC prognosis was assessed using Kaplan‑Meier curves and proportional hazards model (Cox) analysis.
Gene set enrichment analysis was performed by using a Gene Expression Omnibus dataset.
Multi Experiment Matrix was used to predict genes that may be co‑expressed with ROR1‑AS1.
The Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery and KO‑Based Annotation System were used to analyze the most closely associated cytological behaviors and pathways in HCC.
The genes in the three databases were integrated to screen mRNAs, microRNAs and lncRNAs that had co‑expression relationships with ROR1‑AS1.

Cytoscape, Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins and Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis were used to map potential regulatory networks and developmental relationships associated with ROR1‑AS1.
12 genes most closely associated with ROR1‑AS1 were identified, and their relationship was described using a Circos plot.
ROR1‑AS1 was upregulated in HCC, and its expression was related to clinical stage, T stage and N stage.
Kaplan‑Meier curves and Cox analysis indicated that high expression of ROR1‑AS1 was associated with poor prognosis.
ROR1‑AS1 was identified as an independent risk factor for HCC.
Co‑expression data suggested a large regulatory network of 45 genes with indirect associations with ROR1‑AS1.
A small regulatory network of 15 genes with direct or indirect regulatory relationships with ROR1‑AS1 was identified.
A special regulatory network containing 12 genes directly associated with ROR1‑AS1 was identified.
High expression of ROR1‑AS1 suggests poor prognosis in patients with HCC.

MicroRNA hsa-mir-3923 belongs to a type of miRNA, of which the function has been merely investigated in breast, pancreatic cancers and pre-neoplastic stages of gastric cancer.

This study employed data mining for analyzing gastric carcinoma data in The Cancer Genome Atlas database.

The role of hsa-mir-3923 in the prognostic process was assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis, and proportional hazards model (Cox) study.

The common miRNA database was compared to predict potential target genes.

Circos is a highly flexible software package for the circular visualization of complex datasets.
Circos is especially popular in the field of genomic analysis.
Circos enables interactive graphing of analytical data from alternative scientific domains and non-scientific data.
The flexibility of Circos comes with a high degree of complexity.
The complexity of Circos may present an obstacle for researchers not trained in programming or the UNIX command line.
The Galaxy platform provides a user-friendly browser-based graphical interface.
The Galaxy platform incorporates a broad range of 'wrapped' command line tools to facilitate accessibility.
A Galaxy wrapper for Circos has been developed.
The combination of Circos and the Galaxy platform simplifies the specification and configuration of Circos plots for end users.
The combination retains the power to produce publication-quality visualizations of complex multidimensional datasets.
Galactic Circos enables the creation of publication-ready Circos plots using only a web browser via the Galaxy platform.
Users may download the full set of Circos configuration files of their plots for further manual customization.

High throughput next generation sequencing technologies and improved assembly algorithms have resulted in the accumulation of voluminous genomic data in public domains.
The accumulation of genomic data has enabled large scale comparative genome studies, particularly the identification of conserved syntenic blocks among species.
Conserved syntenic blocks facilitate understanding the evolutionary importance of conservation and variation in genomic organization.
Synteny construction and visualization require computational and bioinformatics skills to prepare input files for the synteny analysis pipeline.
Syntenic information in fishes is still in its early stages and is scattered across different research domains.
We present a web-based tool 'Evol2Circos' to provide a user-friendly GUI- and web-based tool for synteny construction and visualization.
Evol2Circos facilitates browsing syntenic information of different fishes using circos, bar, dual, and dot plots.
The information generated from Evol2Circos can be used for further downstream analyses.

Variant allele frequencies (VAF) are an important measure of genetic variation that can be estimated at single-nucleotide variant (SNV) sites.
RNA and DNA VAFs are used as indicators of a wide range of biological traits, including tumor purity and ploidy changes, allele-specific expression, and gene-dosage transcriptional response.
A novel methodology is presented to assess gene and chromosomal allele asymmetries and to aid in identifying genomic alterations in RNA and DNA datasets.
The approach is based on analysis of the VAF distributions in chromosomal segments, which are continuous multi-SNV genomic regions.
In each chromosomal segment, variant probability is estimated as a parameter of a random process that can generate synthetic VAF samples closely resembling the observed data.
Variant probability is a biologically interpretable quantitative descriptor of the VAF distribution in chromosomal segments and is consistent with other approaches.
The proposed methodology is applied to data from 72 samples obtained from patients with breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
DNA and RNA VAF distributions from matched RNA and whole exome sequencing (WES) datasets are compared, showing very similar segmentation and estimated variant probability profiles.
A correlation is found between variant probability and copy number alterations (CNA).
Variant probabilities are used to estimate tumor purity, demonstrating good concordance with other approaches (Pearson's correlation between 0.44 and 0.76).
Variant probabilities can serve as a dependable descriptor of VAF distribution, enabling statistical comparison of matched DNA and RNA datasets.
Variant probabilities provide conceptual and mechanistic insights into relations between the structure of VAF distributions and genetic events.

The methodology is implemented in a Matlab toolbox called GeTallele, which provides functions for analysis, statistical assessment, and visualization of Genome and Transcriptome allele frequency distributions.
GeTallele is available at: https://github.com/SlowinskiPiotr/GeTallele.

The biofuel production involves collecting biomass, breaking down cell wall components, followed by the conversion of sugars to ethanol.
The lignocellulosic biomass comprises 40-50% cellulose, 20-30% hemicellulose, and 10-25% lignin.
Sorghum is a widely adapted energy crop for biofuel production.
Biomass with low lignin, high cellulose, and high hemicellulose contents are exploited to attain maximum biofuel production efficiency.
Resistance to lodging, pest, disease, and abiotic stresses related to cell wall components is well documented.
Quantitative trait loci were identified to understand the genetic correlation of these traits.
Selection for reduced lignin and increased cellulose content in stover can increase the ethanol yield.

Single nucleotide polymorphisms were scanned to identify loci associated with the traits of interest.

In-silico validation of the candidate genes was performed using global gene expression data from large-scale RNA sequencing studies in sorghum available in the NCBI GEO database.
The study aims to evaluate native variations in biofuel-related agronomic traits.
The study aims to evaluate native variations in stalk cell wall components.
The study aims to identify significant SNPs or loci related to cell wall components.
An association mapping panel comprising 245 sorghum minicore germplasm accessions was evaluated.
The evaluation was conducted during two post-rainy seasons of 2013 and 2014.
Observations were recorded on the whole plot for days to 50% flowering.
Observations were recorded on the whole plot for fresh biomass yield (tha).
High broad-sense heritability was exhibited for all the traits in individual seasons.
Significant genotype × environment interaction was observed across seasons except for lignin.
Association mapping was performed with a P < 1×10.
This study reports large variability for agronomic and biofuel traits in the sorghum minicore collection with high heritability.
The genetic architecture of cell wall components using the GWAS approach was studied.
Candidate genes for each cell wall component were annotated.
These results give a better understanding of the genetic basis of the sorghum cell wall composition.
The association analysis identified regions of the genome that could be targeted to enhance the quality of biomass and yield.
The identified regions promote breeding efficiency for enhanced biofuel yield.
Gene co-expression network (GCN) mining identifies gene modules with highly correlated expression profiles across samples/conditions.
GCN mining enables researchers to discover latent gene/molecule interactions.
GCN mining helps identify novel gene functions.
GCN mining extracts molecular features from certain disease/condition groups.
GCN mining helps identify disease biomarkers.
There lacks an easy-to-use tool package for users to mine GCN modules that are relatively small in size with tightly connected genes.

GCN modules may share common members.

TSUNAMI supports data types such as microarray, RNA-seq, or any other numerical omics data.

TSUNAMI has a user-friendly interface and provides real-time co-expression network mining through a web server.

TSUNAMI provides links to other gene set enrichment tools.

Clustering is the process of grouping different data objects based on similar properties.
Clustering has applications in various case studies from several fields such as graph theory, image analysis, pattern recognition, and statistics.
There are numerous algorithms and tools able to generate clustering results.
Different algorithms or parameterizations may produce quite dissimilar cluster sets.
The user is often forced to manually filter and compare clustering results to decide which generate the ideal clusters.
This study presents VICTOR, the first fully interactive and dependency-free visual analytics web application for comparing clustering results.
VICTOR allows the visual comparison of the results of various clustering algorithms.
VICTOR can handle multiple cluster set results simultaneously and compare them using ten different metrics.
Clustering results can be filtered and compared using data tables, interactive heatmaps, bar plots, correlation networks, sankey plots, and circos plots.
VICTOR's functionality is demonstrated using three examples.
In the first example, five different network clustering algorithms are compared on a Yeast protein-protein interaction dataset.
In the second example, four different parameters of the MCL clustering algorithm are tested on the same dataset.
In the third example, four different meta-analyses with hierarchically clustered differentially expressed genes involved in myocardial infarction are compared.
VICTOR is available at http://victor.pavlopouloslab.info or http://bib.fleming.gr:3838/VICTOR.
Type B adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are iatrogenic immune-mediated syndromes with mechanistic etiologies that remain incompletely understood.

Some of the most severe ADRs, including delayed drug hypersensitivity reactions, are T-cell mediated, restricted by specific human leukocyte antigen risk alleles and sometimes by public or oligoclonal T-cell receptors (TCRs).
T-cell receptors (TCRs) are central to the immunopathogenesis of tissue-damaging responses in severe ADRs.
The specific cellular signatures of effector, regulatory, and accessory immune populations that mediate disease, define reaction phenotype, and determine severity have not been defined.

Recent development of single-cell platforms bringing together advances in genomics and immunology provides tools to simultaneously examine the full transcriptome, TCRs, and surface protein markers of highly heterogeneous immune cell populations at the site of the pathological response at a single-cell level.

The requirement for advanced bioinformatics expertise and computational hardware and software has often limited the ability of investigators with the understanding of diseases and biological models to exploit these new approaches.
We describe the features and use of a state-of-the-art, fully integrated application for analysis and visualization of multiomic single-cell data called Visual Genomics Analysis Studio (VGAS).
VGAS is a unique user-friendly, Windows-based graphical user interface specifically designed to enable investigators to interrogate their own data.
VGAS includes tools for sequence alignment and identification of associations with host or organism genetic polymorphisms.

VGAS enables analysis of single-cell TCR-RNA-Cellular Indexing of Transcriptomes and Epitopes by Sequencing (CITE-seq), allowing holistic cellular characterization by unbiased transcriptome and select surface proteome.

VGAS does not require user-directed coding or access to high-performance computers, instead incorporating performance-optimized hidden code to provide application-based fast and intuitive tools for data analyses and production of high-resolution publication-ready graphics on standard specification laptops.
VGAS allows analyses of comprehensive single-cell TCR sequencing (scTCR-seq) data, detailing functional pairings of α-β heterodimer TCRs.
VGAS provides one-click histograms to display entropy and gene rearrangements.
VGAS generates Circos and Sankey plots to visualize clonality and dominance.

For unbiased single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses, VGAS enables users to extract cell transcriptome signatures according to global structure via principal component analysis, t-distributed stochastic neighborhood embedding, or uniform manifold approximation and projection plots.
VGAS allows overlay of scTCR-seq data to identify and select immunodominant TCR-expressing populations.
VGAS integrates sequence-based detection of surface protein markers using oligo-labeled antibodies (CITE-seq) to provide comparative understanding of surface protein expression.
VGAS enables differential gene or protein analyses visualized using volcano plot or heatmap functions.

VGAS allows comparison of data to reference cell atlases or suitable controls to reveal discrete disease-specific subsets, from epithelial to tissue-resident memory T-cells, and activation status, from senescence through exhaustion.
VGAS enables visualization of more finite transcript expression using violin and box plots.
Guided tutorial videos are available for VGAS, as are regular application updates based on the latest advances in bioinformatics and user feedback.
The dramatic development of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies has spurred research interest in decoding cell-cell communication.
Several in-silico methods have been developed to study cell-cell communication.
Most existing methods lack the ability to predict communication pathways connecting the insides and outsides of cells.
CellCall is a toolkit developed to infer inter- and intracellular communication pathways by integrating paired ligand-receptor and transcription factor (TF) activity.
CellCall uses an embedded pathway activity analysis method to identify significantly activated pathways involved in intercellular crosstalk between certain cell types.
CellCall offers a rich suite of visualization options, including Circos plot, Sankey plot, bubble plot, and ridge plot, to present analysis results.

Case studies on scRNA-seq datasets of human testicular cells and the tumor immune microenvironment demonstrated the reliable and unique functionality of CellCall in intercellular communication analysis and internal TF activity exploration.
The functionality of CellCall in intercellular communication analysis and internal TF activity exploration was further validated experimentally.
Comparative analysis of CellCall and other tools indicated that CellCall was more accurate and offered more functions.
CellCall provides a sophisticated and practical tool for deciphering intercellular communication and related internal regulatory signals based on scRNA-seq data.
CellCall is freely available at https://github.com/ShellyCoder/cellcall.
Whole genome and exome sequencing (WGS/WES) are the most popular next-generation sequencing (NGS) methodologies.
WGS/WES are often used to detect rare and common genetic variants of clinical significance.
Automated sequence data processing, management, and visualization should be an indispensable component of modern WGS and WES data analysis.
Automated sequence data processing is essential for sequence assembly, variant detection (SNPs, SVs), imputation, and resolution of haplotypes.
A newly developed findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) bioinformatics-genomics pipeline, Java-based Whole Genome/Exome Sequence Data Processing Pipeline (JWES), is presented.
JWES is designed for efficient variant discovery, interpretation, and big data modeling and visualization.
JWES is a cross-platform, user-friendly, product line application with three modules: (a) data processing, (b) storage, and (c) visualization.
The data processing module performs tasks for variant calling.

A tandem repeat is a sequence of nucleotides that appear as multiple contiguous, near-identical copies arranged consecutively.

EquiRep uses the resulting equivalence classes and consecutive position information to build a weighted graph.

These capabilities underscore EquiRep's broad utility in tandem repeat analysis.

Extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA) has transitioned from genomic curiosity to a pivotal regulator at the intersection of genomics and immunology.
This review synthesizes recent advances in eccDNA biology, elucidating its integral roles in both innate and adaptive immunity and its pathogenic contributions to autoimmune diseases.
eccDNA arises from diverse genomic events, including DNA damage repair, replication stress, and chromothripsis.

In innate immunity, eccDNA functions as a potent damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP), activating cytosolic sensors like cGAS-STING and AIM2 to drive type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine responses.

In the adaptive immune system, eccDNA is not merely a byproduct of processes such as V(D)J recombination (e.g., TRECs, KRECs); it also acts as an active modulator regulating immune gene expression via enhancer-like activity, influencing antigen presentation, and shaping T and B cell development.
Aberrant eccDNA accumulation is implicated in the pathogenesis of autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Plasma eccDNA levels not only correlate with clinical disease activity indices but also track with therapeutic response, positioning eccDNA as a powerful non-invasive biomarker.
Targeting eccDNA biogenesis or its sensing pathways represents a promising therapeutic frontier for restoring immune homeostasis.
Future research integrating single-cell omics and longitudinal profiling is poised to dissect cell-specific functions and unlock the full clinical potential of eccDNA.

Collectively, these findings establish eccDNA as both a functional regulator and a diagnostic tool, offering novel insights into the fundamental interplay between genomic integrity and immune function.
Phylogenetic trees are central to biology.
Most published phylogenetic trees are available only as visual diagrams and not in the machine-readable Newick format.
Thousands of published phylogenetic trees in the scientific literature are unavailable for follow-up analyses, comparisons, and supertree construction.
Experts can easily read phylogenetic tree diagrams.
The manual construction of a Newick string from a diagram is laborious, error-prone, and time-consuming.
Previous attempts to semi-automate the reading of tree images relied on image processing techniques.

Image processing techniques often encounter difficulties with typical published tree diagrams containing various graphical elements and annotations that overlap the branches, such as error bars on internal nodes.
Treemble is a user-friendly desktop application for generating Newick strings from tree images.
The user of Treemble simply clicks to mark node locations, assisted by a deep learning-based node detection tool.
Treemble algorithmically assembles the tree from the node coordinates alone.
Treemble facilitates the automatic reading of tip name labels.
Treemble can be used for both rectangular and circular trees.
Treemble is a native desktop application for macOS and Windows.
Treemble is freely available with documentation at treemble.org.
The source code for Treemble is available at github.com/John-Allard/Treemble.
The trained node detection model is available at huggingface.co/John-Allard/treemble-1.

The symbiotic bacterium Xenorhabdus magdalenensis has a complex life cycle that alternates between a mutualistic relationship with the native entomopathogenic nematode Steinernema australe and a pathogenic stage with the insect host.

The strain is a potential candidate for the development of new-generation biopesticides.

Synthetic genomics is advancing from microbial toward multicellular organisms.
Current manual methods for DNA and genome assembly remain inadequate for the efficient, large-scale production of long DNA constructs.
We present Programmed DNA Assembly via Cas9 and Conjugative Transfer (PACT).
PACT integrates a linear vector system, bacterial conjugation, and programmable Cas9-mediated cleavage to achieve highly efficient, iterative assembly of large DNA fragments.
PACT enhances assembly efficiency by ~30-fold compared to conventional circular vector strategies.
PACT enables one-step assembly of DNA up to 80 kb.
We engineered four single guide-RNA-Marker donor cassettes to support iterative assembly workflows.
PACT can utilize low-recombination Escherichia coli strains as hosts to efficiently assemble Arabidopsis thaliana mitochondrial genome with high repeat units.
Integrated with an automated robotic platform, we developed an unattended, high-throughput pipeline (aPACT) toward large-scale parallel DNA assembly.
Using aPACT, we successfully assembled three large DNA constructs: a 210 kb digital DNA, the designed chloroplast (120 kb) and mitochondrial (350 kb) genome of A. thaliana.
This automated system offers a powerful tool for scalable assembly of large DNA molecules.
This system accelerates synthetic genomics research toward complex multicellular organisms.

Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing have enabled large-scale detection of heteroplasmic variants.

Existing tools often focus on single-sample visualization or require substantial manual preprocessing, limiting their scalability and usability for large cohorts.

MAF data from multiple samples are aggregated into a unified matrix aligned by genomic position.
The unified matrix enables direct cross-sample comparison.
The pipeline provides interactive two-dimensional circular plots that map MAF onto the mitochondrial genome with gene-level annotations.
The circular plots facilitate rapid identification of mutation hotspots and sample-specific patterns.
Mito_Plot offers optional three-dimensional visualizations.
The three-dimensional visualizations enhance exploration of large cohorts by separating variant distributions across samples and genomic regions.
Application of Mito_Plot to multi-sample mitochondrial sequencing datasets demonstrated robust handling of both variants with low and high MAF values.
Mito_Plot demonstrated efficient processing of large cohorts.
Mito_Plot demonstrated improved interpretability compared with static or single-sample visualizations.

Mito_Plot integrates standardized MAF calculation with interactive 2D and 3D visualizations.
Mito_Plot facilitates comprehensive exploration of mitochondrial variant landscapes across large datasets.
The open-source and modular design of Mito_Plot supports reproducible research.

Mito_Plot is a practical resource for mitochondrial genomics research and clinical investigations.

The global prevalence of metabolic diseases (MetDs) continues to rise and is associated with an increased cancer risk.
Genome-wide association studies have identified numerous single nucleotide variants (SNVs) linked to MetDs.
Some single nucleotide variants linked to MetDs are within genes also implicated in tumorigenesis.
G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA secondary structures that regulate gene expression in diverse and context-dependent ways.
Variants affecting G4 structure may alter transcriptional efficiency.
Disease-associated variants are frequently located within or near regulatory elements.
Disease-associated variants may overlap with cancer-associated alternative promoters.
We systematically assess the overlap between MetD-associated SNVs and G4 motifs.
We evaluate the effects of MetD-associated SNVs on G4 stability, topology, and their potential to modulate the regulatory activity of G4s in alternative promoters.
Approximately 0.9% to 1.6% of MetD-associated SNVs are located within G4 motifs (G4-SNVs), depending on the prediction tool.
Effect alleles, those associated with risk or protection against MetDs, generally reduce G4 stability, regardless of their direction of association.
Several G4-SNVs are mapped to cancer-associated alternative promoters.
The destabilizing MICB rs2855804 C/T variant is mapped to a cancer-associated alternative promoter.

In vivo G4 formation is confirmed by permanganate/S1 nuclease footprinting coupled with sequencing.

Integration of Hi-C data, histone modifications, transcription factor binding, and luciferase reporter assays further support the regulatory impact of G4-SNVs.
G4-SNVs are unlikely to be the sole disease drivers.
G4-SNVs significantly influence transcriptional regulation.

G4-SNVs are linked to increased cancer risk in MetD patients.

There is a need for a digital tool that enables continuous and real-time data collection.
A digital tool can help overcome stigma and improve mental health awareness.
We describe mHealth, an open-source, scalable mobile health application.
The mHealth application is compatible with iPhone operating systems (iOS) and Android.
We present details about the pilot phase of the mHealth application.
The mHealth application was built using Xamarin, an open-source framework.

Passive data included pedometer, location, device usage (calls, text, application usage), and location networks.

113 participants (110 iOS testers and 3 Android testers) participated in the mHealth pilot.

We present detailed descriptive data from a participant to illustrate the types of data that can be extracted from the mobile application.

Cell and gene therapy (CGT) manufacturing has outpaced traditional chemistry, manufacturing, and controls frameworks, leaving a 'black box' in vector quality control (QC).

Legacy assays such as Sanger and short-read next-generation sequencing often fail to resolve complex structures including adeno-associated virus (AAV) inverted terminal repeats, lentiviral recombination, and mRNA poly(A) tails.
Oxford Nanopore Technologies enables long-read, native single-molecule sequencing to access these attributes directly.
This review summarizes nanopore sequencing across the CGT lifecycle.
For plasmid DNA, nanopore sequencing confirms full-length circular identity and reveals structural heterogeneity missed by restriction mapping.

For viral vectors (AAV and lentivirus), nanopore sequencing functions as an integrity assay to distinguish full genomes from truncations and to detect sequence-resolved impurities, including reverse-packaged plasmid backbones.
For mRNA therapeutics, direct RNA sequencing profiles poly(A) tail length distributions and base modifications.
Rhodotorula toruloides is an emerging oleaginous yeast with strong potential as a microbial cell factory for the production of acetyl-CoA-derived bioproducts.
Engineering of R. toruloides has been limited by the absence of a functional episomal plasmid system.
A functional episomal plasmid system is a foundational genetic tool for rapid gene expression, pathway testing, and CRISPR-based genome engineering.
We report the first episomal plasmid system for R. toruloides.
Through systematic screening of candidate autonomously replicating sequences (ARSs) from diverse sources, we identified multiple functional ARS elements.
We selected C63F4, a fragment derived from Contig 63 of R. toruloides CBS14, because of its stable performance.
The resulting pC63F4 plasmid was maintained episomally, supported GFP reporter expression, exhibited a copy number of 2.39 ± 0.13, and showed good stability during long term cultivation.
To overcome poor transformation efficiency, we developed a Cre-loxP-mediated in vivo re-circularization strategy that enabled reliable delivery of the episomal plasmid.

Using this improved system, we demonstrated functional episomal expression of metabolic engineering genes and multi-gene pathways for the production of triacetic acid lactone, fatty alcohols, and limonene.
We leveraged this platform to establish a redesigned CRISPR system that enables seamless genome editing in R. toruloides for the first time.

This work establishes a long-needed episomal plasmid platform and associated CRISPR toolkit that will accelerate metabolic engineering, synthetic biology, and fundamental studies in R. toruloides.
Genome-based bacterial taxonomy requires standardized and reproducible analytical workflows for species delineation and phylogenomic placement.

The practical deployment of tools like Prokka, antiSMASH, and PhyloPhlAn in routine laboratory settings, especially on Windows-based systems, remains non-trivial due to complex software dependencies and command-line centric workflows.
Existing solutions, including cloud-based platforms such as Galaxy and KBase, and commercial software suites such as CLC Genomics Workbench, partially alleviate these challenges.

Cloud-based platforms and commercial software suites may involve considerations related to data-privacy concerns, upload latency, storage quotas, shared computing resources, and recurring licensing costs.
We introduce TaxaScope, a graphical-interface-driven desktop workstation designed to support reproducible, genome-based bacterial taxonomy.

cpEXLA represents an intriguing native tool for studying cell wall evolution and the functional role of EXLAs.

Secondary infection is a significant complication of snakebite envenomation.

One review focused on identifying bacteria present in the oral cavity of snakes.

theBIGbam can compress hundreds of gigabytes of input files 10- to 100-fold into dedicated databases while retaining key per-position information.

theBIGbam is designed to complement existing browsing tools like IGV and Anvi'o.
